title: India Rejects UN Report Calling Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company 'India-Based'
excerpt: New Delhi told a UN committee the description ignores the Security Council's own record: Dawood Ibrahim has been wanted in India for terror attacks since 1993 and fled the country long before his 2003 listing.
body:
• India has strongly rejected a UN special rapporteur's description of Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company as an "India-based" criminal group, calling it a glaring inaccuracy.
  • First Secretary Raghoo Puri told the UN General Assembly's Third Committee that Dawood has been wanted in India for terror attacks since 1993 and fled the country before his 2003 Security Council listing.
  • New Delhi said rapporteur Ben Saul's report omitted facts recorded in the UN's own 1267 sanctions narrative summary.
  • India warned that unaccountable factual errors by UN mandate holders cause the organisation "tremendous harm."

India has strongly rejected a United Nations special rapporteur's description of Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company as an "India-based" criminal group, telling a UN committee the phrase reverses the basic facts of the case: the organisation's leader is a fugitive from Indian justice, wanted for terror attacks since 1993.

Raghoo Puri, First Secretary in India's Permanent Mission to the UN, delivered the rebuttal on Wednesday in the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly, responding to a report by Ben Saul, the Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

What the report said, and what India says it omitted

Puri noted that Saul's report stated that in 2003 the Security Council listed the leader of one criminal group, "the India-based D-Company," for association with Al-Qaeda. Taken alone, he argued, the line implies the network operates from India.

https://x.com/mid_day/status/2113183436269838443

"Read in isolation, this line paints a very different picture from the actual reality."

— Raghoo Puri, First Secretary, India's Permanent Mission to the UN

India's objection is that the report left out what the UN's own sanctions record states. The narrative summary under the Security Council's 1267 Al-Qaeda sanctions regime records that D-Company and Dawood Ibrahim have been wanted in India in connection with terror attacks since 1993 — the year of the Mumbai serial blasts. Dawood fled India well before the 2003 listing, Puri said, and it was from outside the country that he was designated for association with Al-Qaeda and Osama bin Laden. Indian officials have long maintained that he is sheltered in Pakistan, a charge Islamabad denies.

A wider complaint about accountability

The exchange went beyond one phrase. Puri said India's delegation has raised concerns in other forums about special rapporteurs releasing reports containing factual inaccuracies without being held accountable for them, presenting member states with a fait accompli — a situation he called unfortunate for an organisation already facing challenges to its legitimacy.

"Not mentioning this fact is regrettable, and such incompetence on the part of special mandate holders does this organisation tremendous harm."

— Raghoo Puri, First Secretary, India's Permanent Mission to the UN

Special rapporteurs are independent experts appointed by the UN Human Rights Council; they are not UN staff and are not paid directly by the organisation. That independence, India argues, makes accuracy and impartiality in their published reports more important, not less, because their findings are widely cited by governments, courts and media. Reporting by IANS said New Delhi also hit out at what it saw as bias in the counter-terrorism report and called for high standards of impartiality.

Why the wording matters

For India, the label is not a pedantic dispute. How UN documents describe terror-linked networks shapes how other countries treat them — in sanctions enforcement, extradition arguments and diplomatic exchanges with Pakistan. Describing D-Company as "India-based" blurs the distinction New Delhi has drawn for three decades: that the network attacked India from outside its territory and that its leader remains beyond India's reach precisely because he is not in India.

India has raised similar objections before when international reports described Pakistan-based groups in ways it considered misleading. There was no immediate public response from Saul's office to Wednesday's statement. Whether the report is corrected or annotated will be the next test of the accountability question India put on the record.
